text: This lesson is intentionally brief — an orientation, not a deep dive, exactly as the title says. You've already done the heavy lifting on Snowflake and Databricks; BigQuery and Redshift get a lighter pass here. The goal is simple: recognize their SQL when you see it, not master every feature.

Google's BigQuery uses what Google calls Standard SQL — not the older, now-legacy dialect BigQuery originally shipped with. If you're looking at current BigQuery work, Standard SQL is what you're seeing. Its most distinctive visual signature: fully-qualified table names in backticks, spanning project, dataset, and table all at once. Select customer id, order date, total due, from backtick my-project dot sales_dataset dot orders backtick. Spot that three-part backtick-quoted name and you know immediately you're looking at BigQuery.

BigQuery also has native array and struct types built right into the column itself — tags as an array of strings, or address as a struct, a nested record, reached with ordinary dot notation: address dot city, address dot zip. A single column holding a repeated value or a nested record directly is a distinctly BigQuery pattern among the platforms in this course.

Now Redshift, which is the easiest platform in this entire course if you already know PostgreSQL — because Redshift genuinely IS built on an older fork of Postgres. Select customer id, order date, total due, from orders, where order date is greater than or equal to a date, limit 10. That reads almost exactly like plain PostgreSQL. Of every warehouse dialect covered in this course, Redshift requires the least new learning if PostgreSQL is already familiar to you.

One more thing worth knowing about Redshift, even though we won't go deep on it: it layers its own distribution-key and sort-key concepts onto CREATE TABLE — DISTKEY of customer id, SORTKEY of order date — controlling how data physically spreads across compute nodes and how it's ordered on disk. This is real, genuine Redshift syntax. But it's an administration and physical-design concern, not a language-comparison one, so it sits outside this course's scope on purpose.

To recap: BigQuery uses Standard SQL with backtick-qualified project-dataset-table names and native array/struct types; Redshift is the closest thing to PostgreSQL you'll find anywhere in this course, with DISTKEY and SORTKEY as its own administration-layer extensions on top. Next lesson closes this chapter with a genuinely interesting observation: why cloud warehouse dialects, as a group, converge with each other more than the older OLTP platforms ever have.
